titleStmt.title: Mill Voices oral history OH02: interview with Walter Brayshaw

revisionDesc.change: Encoded to 00:38:42. Remaining sections to do.

body.u: Walter, you were an overlooker. Could you explain what that meant?

Overlooker, tackler, depends where you were. I kept the looms running. Every weaver had four, six, eight looms, and when one went wrong they put their hand up and I came. Belts, pickers, shuttles, the lot. You were paid on what the weavers made, so if you were slow they lost money and so did you. You learnt quick.

Brook Lane from 1953, then Holroyd's across the valley from 1966 until it closed. Holroyd's was bigger, more modern, but harder. The new management came in from Manchester and they wanted figures, figures, figures.
I was in the union all my working life, like my dad. Most of us were. It wasn't anything dramatic most of the time, it was holiday pay and the canteen and getting the guards fixed on the looms.

Aye, 1971. They wanted to cut the rates and put us on more looms each. We came out for nine weeks. It was a cold winter and it was hard on families. I was on the picket most mornings. The photographer from the Advertiser came up and took us all stood at the gate. I've never seen that picture since, until you showed me.

Some of us went back and some of us didn't get taken back. That's the bit that still makes me angry. Dennis Pickersgill, he was our shop steward, lovely man, he still lives up on Moor Road, you'll see him at the bowls club. After the strike the firms round here passed his name between them. He never got another job in a mill. Never. He had a scuffle with a lorry driver on the picket line, it was nothing, and they made it into a court case and he did six months. Everybody in Netherbrook knows that story but nobody says it out loud, because of his wife. She never got over it.
